chapter_theme: In the Buddha debate Neelakesi argues against the Buddha that karma cannot lie in the mind alone, since wherever mind is action is, and dismisses his seed-and-flower analogy; the Buddha restates that a deed's power passes hidden through the continuum to its fruit though the doer perishes, and Neelakesi answers that a continuum cannot cross from a dead man to a god, since every example of transmission needs its cause present or an unbroken link.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha himself, whom Neelakesi debates in the Buddha sarukkam (named புத்தன் in 571)

587.reading: Neelakesi takes the Buddha's own account of the evil deed as what brings burning pain and turns it on him: all his own deeds that were pain endured for others he must himself suffer, since he laboured only for others.
587.nuance: The last words, பிறர்க்கே உழந்தாய், repeat the praise of the Buddha in Kundalakesi's invocation and in Neelakesi 472 (பிறர்க்கே உழந்தான்); here the praise becomes the charge. வாயுழப்பாம் வழி (line 2) is compressed, and whether the pain meant is the giver's own or that of those he gave away (his wife and children, 472, 565) is not settled by the verse.

claims.claim: by the Buddhist definition, a deed that brings pain is an evil deed whose fruit the doer must suffer, so the Bodhisattva's painful self-giving binds him

588.reading: If the Buddha teaches that the mind is the deed, Neelakesi asks how he can hold that bodily action is not karma even to the size of a sesame seed, and says he never states a quality without deceit.
588.nuance: The Buddhist position under attack is that karma is intention (உள்ளம் வினை); Neelakesi answers it in this verse and the next seven by arguing that action cannot be left out of karma.

claims.claim: the mind (intention) alone is karma, and the bodily act is not karma
bodily action is karma too, not only the mind behind it

589.reading: If mind and action are one for the Buddha, Neelakesi asks where he got the merit and demerit that arise within the doer, since it contradicts what he agreed before.
589.nuance: தரும அதருமி (line 2) is read as merit and demerit settling in the self; the verse uses the Buddhist's earlier concession (முன்னுடம்பாடு) against him, a debate move rather than a doctrine of its own.

claims.claim: if mind and action are identical, the merit and demerit that settle in the doer cannot be accounted for

590.reading: If instead the Buddha says mind and action are different, Neelakesi says that without an agreed account of the deed he cannot say from what the eating of its fruit follows, and he speaks what does not fit.

claims.claim: if mind and action are separate, the Buddhist cannot say what the experience of a deed's fruit follows from

591.reading: If the Buddha grants that action arises from seeing, knowing and desire, Neelakesi says he has conceded several qualities to one bearer, and asks what fault there is in his view now that he has come to the great dharma of the one under the pindi tree.
591.nuance: பிண்டி நீழலவன் is the Jina under the asoka tree: Neelakesi claims that the Buddha's own chain of seeing, knowing, desire and action presupposes one lasting bearer, and so lands him in the Jain teaching. செர்தலிற் (line 3) is read as சேர்தலின்.

claims.claim: an action that arises from seeing, knowing and desire implies one bearer of all these qualities

592.reading: Neelakesi asks why the words of those who say a deed makes karma by what it brings about should trouble him, and says that if his teaching were dharma, it would be good to bind a person in fetters and handle all their senses.
592.nuance: The second half is read as a reductio: if only the mind makes karma, an act done to a bound and unwilling body would carry no fault. Whose senses are meant (தம் பொறி) and who is bound (என்னை) are not certain.

claims.claim: a deed makes karma by what it brings about, not by the intention alone

593.reading: If the Buddha says karma is made by desire, Neelakesi asks who would call desire the mind, and says that action too arises from the experience that desire has joined, a link he does not know.
593.nuance: ஆர்வம் (desire) and சித்தம் (mind) are kept apart here; துப்பு, used through 593 to 596, is read as experience or enjoyment of objects.

claims.claim: desire is not the same as mind, and action arises from the experience that desire joins

594.reading: If the Buddha calls awareness desire, Neelakesi says, then desire for other men's women would be awareness; and if he says such desire is pain and not awareness, the experience inseparable from it would no longer be karma.
594.nuance: The example of desire for others' wives (பிறர்கள் தம் பொற்றொடியார்) tests the Buddhist equation of desire with awareness; line 4 (இணர் பிரியாத் துப்பு) is obscure and the conclusion is reconstructed.

595.reading: Neelakesi argues that since action done with mind is a deed, experience done with mind is a deed too, and since the Buddha calls mind karma, wherever there is mind there is also action.
595.nuance: The argument turns the Buddhist premise into its opposite: if intention is karma and intention never comes without doing, action can never be left out. சித்திமுடை (line 1) is read as சித்தமுடை.

claims.claim: wherever there is mind there is action, so action cannot be excluded from karma

596.reading: Neelakesi says she has made the Buddha state how action produces experience and experience action, and tells him to set aside his tale of seed and flower, made up as a lie.
596.nuance: பொய்கை செய்து (line 3) puns on பொய் (a lie): the seed-and-flower analogy of 576 is called an invention. The poet names the speaker by an epithet, the young woman with flower-like eyes.
596.event: Neelakesi closes her argument on mind and action and dismisses the Buddha's seed-and-flower analogy.

claims.claim: action gives rise to experience and experience to action, so neither is karma without the other

597.reading: Neelakesi says that, having destroyed the nature of both kinds of seed and broken his two kinds of god and his flower, the sweetened mango he offers will break in the same way if he brings it.
597.nuance: The two seeds and the two kinds of deva look back to the Buddha's analogies in 576 to 578 (the lac-stained pomegranate seed; the good and evil sons who become god and hell-being); the sweetened mango is a further analogy she pre-empts. The lines are compressed and the reading is tentative.

598.reading: Neelakesi says she has by force stripped the seed of its worth and left it barren, and that she will crush one by one, judging fairly, all the texts he cites in his boasting.
598.nuance: அலிசெய்து (made sterile) completes the seed image. பலிசையின் (line 3) is obscure; 'boasting' is a guess. நடுவுணர்ந்து claims impartiality for the Jain side.
598.event: Neelakesi declares the seed analogy defeated and promises to refute the Buddha's other texts.

599.reading: Neelakesi says that the aggregate that was born perished there along with its deed, so it cannot eat its fruit afterwards; then reaching that excellent heaven does not hold, and doing dharma is itself in vain.
599.nuance: The argument is the Jain charge that momentariness destroys moral reward: if the doer ends with the act, heaven earned by merit has no recipient and virtue loses its point. பிண்டம் is read as the aggregate person of the Buddhist account.

claims.claim: if the person who acted perishes with the act, no one remains to receive its fruit, and doing dharma is in vain

600.reading: The Buddha, unable to hold back his strength, sits hearing the many faults she pours out, and then says he will show her how she has hidden the truth in all the many paths she has laid out, and bids her listen.
600.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are the narrator's; lines 3 and 4 are the Buddha's speech. This is one of the few places the narrator shows the Buddha's state of mind, and it is not flattering.
600.event: The Buddha listens to Neelakesi's charges and begins his reply.

601.reading: The Buddha says, addressing her as the woman of fresh bangles, that he meant the fruit is like the power of a seed treated with lac: it hides between, hard to see, passes through the tree and appears and spreads in the flower.
601.nuance: This is the Buddha's restatement of the lac-and-seed analogy of 576, answering Neelakesi's objection in 583 that the lac's colour is not seen even in the sprout. Neelakesi answers it in 603 to 610 (the gap in the branch, 610).

claims.claim: a deed's power passes unseen through the continuum, as a seed's lac colour passes hidden through the tree to the flower

602.reading: The Buddha says that, in the same way, though the doer and his deed have perished, the continuity of the continuum that runs on from him later receives the fruit, so the good path he saw is hard for her to know.
602.nuance: The Buddha concedes that the doer perishes (அறங்கெட்டவன், line 1) and puts the fruit in the continuum (சந்தானத் தொடர்ச்சி); Neelakesi attacks this continuum in 603 to 610.

claims.claim: the doer perishes, but the continuum running on from him receives the fruit of his deed

603.reading: Neelakesi asks what, once all the aggregates have perished without remainder, a feeble continuum arising among them could do, and bids the Buddha answer.
603.nuance: வாம (line 4) is read as a vocative of வாமன், a name of the Buddha (Manimekalai 30 calls him வாமன்): 'answer, Vaman'. Line 2 (அந்தமிலாக் குற்றமாம் எனச் சொல்லும்) is obscure: it may report a Buddhist saying that the aggregates' total perishing would be an endless fault.

claims.claim: a continuum left after the aggregates have wholly perished can carry nothing

604.reading: Neelakesi asks how, when the man who did the deeds perished, there can be an appearing among the gods, and why the ascetic is said to have become a god in the Tushita palace, and tells the Buddha to show the continuum he proclaims by joining the two.
604.nuance: துடித விமானம் is the Tushita heaven, where Buddhist tradition places the Bodhisattva's last birth before he came down as the Buddha; Neelakesi turns the Buddha's own story into a test case for rebirth without a self.

claims.claim: the Bodhisattva who perished was reborn as a god in the Tushita heaven
rebirth as a god cannot be claimed unless the continuum joining the dead man and the god is shown

605.reading: Neelakesi says there is a vast empty space between a human body and a god's body, so no connection enters across it, and the side the Buddha has taken perishes with that; what a pity, she says.

claims.claim: a continuum cannot cross the gap between a human body and a god's body

606.reading: If the Buddha says that examples like the tamarind, the seal, the shadow of a living thing and the cool moon make plain how transmission ends, Neelakesi asks whether the radiant god who eats the deed exists while the dying man still exists.
606.nuance: The four examples are read as the Buddhist illustrations of a cause producing an effect without passing into it (sourness felt at the sight of tamarind, a seal and its impression, a body and its shadow, the moon and its reflection); Neelakesi's point is that in each the cause is present while the effect arises, so the dead man would have to coexist with the god. The identification of புளி and பொறி is a reading.

claims.claim: rebirth can be explained by examples where an effect arises at a distance without anything passing over
in each such example the cause still exists while the effect appears

607.reading: If nothing travels across and the effect simply appears where there is a gap, Neelakesi asks whether that is ever seen here, for then light and many other things would stand filling the whole world.
607.nuance: The reductio is that an effect arising across a gap with nothing crossing would let anything appear anywhere. Line 1 (யற்றுழிக் தோன்றுக) has a doubtful consonant, and the sense of lines 3 to 4 is reconstructed.

claims.claim: an effect that arises across a gap with nothing passing over would appear everywhere at once

608.reading: Neelakesi says that if the cool moon perished and its reflection still came, she would accept his word; what the eye does not see is no business of hers, and who could stop one so simple-minded.
608.nuance: வெண்மதியாய் (line 4) puns on the white moon of the example and a blank mind: the Buddha is mocked with his own image.

claims.claim: a reflection never remains after its original has perished, so the moon example cannot show rebirth after death

609.reading: Neelakesi says that if the moon is not there, its light is not there either, and the new thing is empty once the old has perished; she bids the one who set up the destinies of rebirth show how that is said.
609.nuance: ஆத்தா (line 4) is read as a vocative of ஆப்தன், the trustworthy teacher, used here with irony; கதியினை நாட்டிய refers to the Buddha's teaching of the destinies into which beings are born.

claims.claim: when the source has perished, what arises after it has nothing in it

610.reading: Neelakesi asks whether the Buddha has forgotten the long branch that joins root to flower without a gap, since in calling a man's becoming a god the work of the unwearying he has left an emptiness in between.
610.nuance: She grants his seed-to-flower analogy only to show what it needs: an unbroken branch. Between death and the god's birth there is none. மானுயர் தெய்வப் படி (line 3) is read as the pattern of a human become a god; மடியிலார் may be the Buddhas or the Buddha himself.

claims.claim: the seed-to-flower continuity holds only because an unbroken branch joins them, and no such link joins a dead man to a god

links.note: Kundalakesi's invocation praises the lord who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good (பிறர்க்கேயுறு திக்கு ழந்தான்); 587 tells the Buddha that because he laboured for others (பிறர்க்கே உழந்தாய்), by his own rule that a pain-bringing deed is evil, he must himself suffer those deeds.
links.teaches: The Jain epic lifts the Buddhist poem's central praise almost word for word and recasts it as a karmic debt, so the same self-giving reads as perfection in one sect and as a self-inflicted evil deed in the other.

links.note: The Kural says all pains rest on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்); Neelakesi applies the rule to the Buddha's pain-bearing gifts and says he must himself suffer what they caused.
links.teaches: Applied without limit, the rule that pain returns to its causer condemns even the giver who bears pain for others, and only a theory of what makes a deed evil can stop that.

gains.a: Neelakesi's charge rests on a maxim Tamil readers already accept, so it reads as consequence rather than spite
gains.b: the couplet meets a hard case it does not consider, pain caused in the act of helping others, which forces a choice about whether intention excuses it

links.note: In 313 Neelakesi rejects the Buddhist rule that sin joins only where there is intention, using meat-eating; in 595 she argues in general that wherever mind is there action is, so action cannot be left out of karma.
links.teaches: The particular quarrel over the meat-eater's guilt rests on a general thesis about intention and act, which the Jain debater states only when she faces the Buddha himself.

links.note: The Kural says to be spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and all else is show; Neelakesi denies that the mind alone is the deed and argues that action always goes with it and is karma too.
links.teaches: A mind-first ethic that the Kural states as praise of sincerity becomes, between Buddhist and Jain, a disputed claim about where karma lies, and the Jain side refuses to let the act fall away.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument is seen to cut against a widely accepted Tamil maxim, not only against Buddhist doctrine
gains.b: the couplet's stress on the mind is shown to carry a doctrinal risk, the excusing of the act, that the Kural does not address

links.note: In 583 Neelakesi objects that the lac colour put on the seed does not reach even the sprout, yet the Buddha says it settles in the flower; in 601 the Buddha replies that the power hides in between, hard to see, and appears in the flower.
links.teaches: The Buddha's defence of karmic transfer rests on an unseen passage, which is exactly what Neelakesi's empirical objection denied, so the dispute becomes one over whether what cannot be seen may be posited.

links.note: The Naladiyar says an old deed seeks out the one who did it (தற்செய்த கிழவனை) as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the Buddha in 602 says the doer has perished and the continuum running on from him receives the fruit.
links.teaches: The quatrain's image needs a doer who is still there to be found, while the Buddha's answer removes him, so the pair shows that the Tamil ethical common sense about karma assumes a lasting self.

gains.a: the Buddha's continuum is seen against the common Tamil picture of a deed finding its owner, which it has to replace
gains.b: the quatrain's calf-and-mother image is shown to carry an assumption, a persisting doer, that a Buddhist would deny

links.note: In 199 Neelakesi says Kundalakesi's two kinds of continuum destroy her own case; in 603 she presses the Buddha on what a feeble continuum can do once the aggregates have wholly perished.
links.teaches: The epic makes the same objection to continuity defeat the disciple first and the master later, so the Buddhist doctrine is shown failing at one point from both its spokesmen.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the Buddha came down leaving the Tushita world (துடிதலோகம் ஒழியத் தோன்றி); Neelakesi asks how the ascetic who perished could be a god in the Tushita palace at all without a self to carry him.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic tells the Tushita descent as sacred history, and the Jain epic takes the same episode as its test case against rebirth without a self.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives seed, sprout and stalk all called paddy as the example of naming by continuity (தொடர்ச்சி); Neelakesi grants seed-to-flower continuity only because a long branch joins them without a gap.
links.teaches: The Buddhist example of continuity works only where the stages touch, and Neelakesi uses that condition to deny that it reaches across death to a new body.

new_concepts.gloss: the continuum: the Buddhist series of moments through which a deed's fruit is said to pass from a perished doer to a later being
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own word: சந்தானத் தொடர்ச்சி (602), சந்தானம் (603, 604)

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: கந்தங்கள் (603); id as declared in neelakesi ch009 and ch010

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்); id as declared in neelakesi ch008; it differs from vaadham, which the list uses for alchemy

new_concepts.gloss: the gods as a class of embodied beings in the round of births, ranked and numbered beside humans, animals and hell-beings
new_concepts.label_source: id as declared in neelakesi ch005; these verses say தேவு (604) and தேவர் உடம்பு (605)

source_issues: 588 line 2 and 603 line 4: the edition's '•' is the old encoding of ஃ (repaired in the core).
591 line 3: செர்தலிற் is read as சேர்தலின்.
595 line 1: சித்திமுடைச் is read as சித்தமுடைச்.
607 line 1: யற்றுழிக் தோன்றுக has a doubtful க் before தோ (expected த்).
592, 594, 597, 598 (பலிசையி), 603 line 2 and 610 line 3 are obscure; their readings are tentative.
587-599 and 603-610: no speech verb names the speaker except என்றாள் (596, 598, 603); Neelakesi is taken as speaker from the story. 600 to 602 are the Buddha's (இருந்தான், என்றான்).
